Why holiday seasons don’t drive mobile game spending the way you’d expect
Tomas Hubka
Last updated: Nov 23, 2026
min read
Black Friday and the broader holiday season reshape retail revenue every year. In mobile games, the impact is far smaller than most studios assume. Here’s what the data shows across Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Christmas, and the stretch of holidays that follow, and why mobile game monetization follows a different calendar than retail.
Black Friday 2025 pulled in
$11.8 billion in US online sales
. Cyber Monday added
$14.25 billion
. Mobile commerce accounted for more than 57% of Cyber Monday purchases. If you worked in mobile gaming that November, you probably felt the pressure to ship a holiday offer, a seasonal reskin, or a limited-time bundle. And then you probably watched the numbers come in flat.
‍
The gap between what retail does during the holidays and what mobile gaming does is, however, quite big. And the same pattern holds across Christmas, New Year, and the string of seasonal moments that follow. This piece looks at what the data shows across the broader holiday season, drawing on reports from Adobe,
AppsFlyer
,
Adjust
, Sensor Tower,
Moloco
,
AppMagic
, and our own benchmark data across roughly 1,800 paying mobile games.
The retail backdrop
For context on the expectation most studios are working against: Adobe reported total US online spending of
$257.8 billion
between November 1 and December 31, 2025, with mobile commerce accounting for more than half of all online spending. As Vivek Pandya, Lead Analyst at Adobe Digital Insights,
put it
:
‍
Competitive and persistent deals throughout Cyber Week pushed consumers to shop earlier, creating an environment where Black Friday now challenges the dominance of Cyber Monday.
In broad e-commerce terms, the holiday season is a genuine revenue event. It’s the context mobile game teams are working inside when they plan Q4 and where the expectation gap starts.
What mobile games actually see across the holidays
The industry-wide picture is more muted than the retail one. Sensor Tower’s State of Mobile 2026 report put global mobile game spending at
$81.8 billion in 2025
. For context, non-game app spending grew 21% year over year while games grew more slowly, and no new mobile game crossed the $1 billion revenue mark in 2025. The Sensor Tower report described 2025 as a
“year of divergence for mobile gaming.”
Mobile gaming is growing, but not through holiday bursts.
AppsFlyer’s State of Gaming for Marketers 2026 reinforces the same pattern from the UA side.
Based on anonymized data from 9,600 gaming apps
, AppsFlyer found that mobile games spent $25 billion on user acquisition in 2025, up only 3.8% compared to 2024, with iOS rising 6% and Android 2%. For comparison, non-gaming app marketing spend grew 18% to $53 billion in the same period. Shopping category investment alone increased 70% overall and 123% on iOS. The money is flowing into apps that make money from holiday shopping. Mobile games aren’t one of those categories.
PocketGamer.biz reported that US Black Friday mobile game spending reached
roughly $70 million
in a recent benchmark, up 25% year over year. That’s a real signal, but $70 million against an $81.8 billion annual market works out to less than 0.1% of the year in a single day. The holiday matters in a specific regional and platform slice and doesn’t move the global picture.
Tebex, which processes payments for PC and mobile games,
saw 58.9% year-over-year growth on Cyber Monday 2025 and 33.6% on Black Friday
. But Tebex is heavily weighted toward PC, where buying patterns are closer to retail than they are to mobile free-to-play.
Moloco’s seasonality analysis of the 2025 holiday period
describes the pattern clearly
:
‍
Downloads surge in late November around Thanksgiving and Black Friday, then peak over Christmas and New Year at more than 40% above the start of Q4.
‍
Downloads rise clearly. Spending, less so.
Adjust’s analysis of its own 2025 holiday data
noted the same tension
:
‍
The holiday season offers more than short-term spikes. The opportunity now is to operationalize what the data shows.
‍
